The Hexamilion wall was constructed near this city by Theodosius in the fifth century to protect against Visogothic incursions. His reform policies, including the standardization of German as an official language, the abolition of feudalism, and several attacks on church power, encountered opposition, which was especially strong in Hungary. Consequentially, under his successor, Leopold II, the majority of this man's reforms were repealed. FTP name this late 18th century Hapsburg ruler, who succeeded his mother Maria Theresa.

The ideas that he formed were implemented in La Reunion and the New England Community Place. Most of his ideas can be found in his The Theory of the Four Movements, which proposed that humanity would be ruled by an omniarch and live in cities called phalanxes. Influencing people like Robert Owen and George Ripley, name this Utopian theorist from France.

Iara Lee managed to smuggle out footage from this event. Kate Greghart was tasered while attempting to photograph it from onboard the Challenger 1. This politician advanced the idea of his nation as the "Empire of Liberty", and one of his letters states that there should be a "Wall of Separation" between church and state. This person wrote several articles under the pen name of Ralph Robinson. John Bly and Charles Rose were the only two men hanged for their role in this event. Governor Bowdoin drew up a Riot Act suspending habeas corpus to deal with this conflict. General Benjamin Lincoln led an army that killed three rebels in this conflict and prevented the Springfield Armory from being taken. Henry Knox told one of the state officials trying to suppress it that the federal government could not intervene because Congress was not in session. It ended at Petersham and those involved were pardoned within a year by Governor Hancock. Identify this uprising by a Massachusetts soldier which illustrated the flaws of the Articles of Confederation.

Foreign policy actions taken during this man's reign include the dissolution of Manzzini's Roman Republic and the restoration of Pope Pius IX, despite this ruler's earlier sympathies for Italian nationalism. In 1870, following the French defeat at Sedan in the Franco-Prussian War, he was deposed. For 10 points name this man the first president of the French Republic and last Emperor of France, reigning from 1851 until 1870.

Three perpetrators of this action assumed the identities of customs officials immediately before it, while their leader took the codename Apis and was sentenced to death in the Salonika trial. One perpetrator failed to commit suicide by swallowing a cyanide pill and jumping into a four-inch deep river.

James Mason notably had to read a speech drafted by the main opponent of this bill. Henry Foote pulled a gun on another figure during the debate surrounding it. It was created to allow California to enter the Union as a Free State, and it also updated the Fugitive Slave Act. Name this bill that prevented the Civil War from happening for another eleven years.

Positions held by this man included Prince of Benevento, a position he renounced when it was restored to the Papal States. He was removed from his position as the Bishop of Autun because he agreed with the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Anthony Merry and this man opened a line of communication during the negotiation of the Treaty of Amiens, and he pushed for reorganization of the Holy Roman Empire into the Confederation of the Rhine. He was critical of the harsh provisions imposed on Prussia and Austria in the Treaties of Tilsit and Pressburg, and fell out of favor in the later part of Napoleon's reign. However, he later returned to favor under the restored Bourbon monarchy, and served as France's chief negotiator at the 1814 Congress of Vienna. FTP name this French diplomat and cockroach-like political survivor.

One person with this name created a namesake type of literary imitation that supplanted Aristotle's mimesis among Romans like Quintilian. That person wrote a history called Roman Antiquities and was from Halicarnassus. A person with this name led the losing Ionians in the Battle of Lade and was from Phocaea. A person with this name expelled the philosopher Dion under the advice of Plato and was besieged in a citadel on Ortygia by Timoleon. That ruler supposedly had the literal Sword of Damocles hanging over his head, which didn't improve his rule much, and along with an "Elder" father, was a tyrant of Syracuse. Two days of a festival to a god of this name were devoted to dithyrambs. Each participant in that festival created a work featuring Satyrs in the chorus. Name this god to whom Athens dedicated its yearly festival of plays.

One pioneer in this industry used the symbol of a dolphin entwined around an anchor to represent the phrase "festina lente." A book about this industry takes a mosaic approach and analyzes the "darker purpose" of the subdivision of King Lear's kingdom. Johann Fust helped finance an innovation in it before bringing a lawsuit for allegedly unpaid loans. More portable products in this industry were created by the Venetian Aldus Manutius. Only 49 copies of a 42-line object created by this industry survive. This industry became more prominent after cast metal replaced woodblocks. Name this industry that took off after the invention of moveable type by Johannes Gutenberg.

A disheveled woman carrying her drunken husband on her back refuses this historical figure's assistance in Thomas Nast's cartoon "GET THEE BEHIND ME SATAN." After being introduced to spiritualist theology by Colonel James Blood, this person found work in New York City conducting seances for Cornelius Vanderbilt. Anthony Comstock began his anti-obscenity campaign after this person published a salacious article about Elizabeth Tilton's affair with Henry Ward Beecher. With Tennessee Claflin, this advocate of "free love" ran a namesake weekly newspaper and operated the first female-owned brokerage firm on Wall Street. This woman selected Frederick Douglas as her running mate while running as the Equal Rights Party candidate in 1872. Name this first woman to run for president.

A port on this body of water once called Akhtiar was founded by Admiral Thomas MacKenzie. The ship Taif (tah-eef), bearing Adolphus Slade, was the only survivor of a battle in this body of water. Although not Greek, that battle here was the last major battle between sailing ship fleets due to the use of explosive shells. To confine a major fleet to this body of water, the Great Powers signed the 1841 London Convention. To defend one of its ports, Eduard Totleben ordered a fleet sunk to block the harbor, and the subsequent siege ended after the taking of Malakoff Redoubt. Kenneth Pomeranz pointed to the availability of this good in the West to explain the "Great Divergence." After an incident at Silkstone, the 7th Earl of Shaftesbury reformed labor requirements for working with this good, preventing the employment of girls as hurriers and trappers. A form of this good used to do better iron smelting was known as coke. Name this black fuel that helped ignite the Industrial Revolution in Britain.

CIA Station Chief James Angleton manipulated an election determining this position by skimming money from the Exchange Stabilization Fund and exchanging money at the Hassler Hotel. This was the highest position involved in the "Bribesville" scandal and investigated by the "Clean Hands" judges. One holder of this position reconciled with Berlinguer of the Communist Party in the "Historic Compromise." This person presided over the first public meeting of the Society for the Extinction of the Slave Trade at Exeter Hall. This person had the governess Louise Lehzen exiled in a power struggle. This person defeated the Earl of Powis to become Chancellor of the University of Cambridge. This person faced mistrust because he was an ancestor of the German House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. This person's wife wore black for the rest of her life due to grief over his death. Name this Prince consort of Queen Victoria.
Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha

Advocates of this political cause pressured the Senate to override a presidential veto of the Webb-Kenyon Act. St. Gall in Switzerland and St. Denis in Paris are both Benedictine examples of, what building complexes that house communities of monks?

The precedent for this requirement established in Frothingham v. Mellon was overturned in Flast v. Cohen, which resulted in the Flast Test for determining if taxpayers meet this requirement. Defenders of Wildlife established the three part test that established how to meet this requirement, including the need for an "injury in fact." Name this eligibility of a party to file a suit in court.

Due to anger about missile testing, Peter Greyson dumped red paint on a physical copy of this document. This document can be altered using the 7/50 (seven-fifty) formula, and it is subject to he "Living Tree Doctrine." Parts of this document can be overridden under the "notwithstanding clause." Name this document that provides the framework for the governance of a country with a capital at Ottawa.

A Joan Didion essay titled "[this politician] Agonistes" notes how Jesse Jackson once referred to him as "nothing but an appetite." Name this president who had a good relationship with the black community despite the Monica Lewinsky scandal.

Frederick William I received a regiment of dragoons in exchange for giving some of this substance to another ruler. It was first created in Europe by Ehrenfried von Tschirnhaus, who had a factory for producing this substance in Meissen. The Zwinger Palace holds 20,000 objects made from this substance collected by Augustus the Strong in Dresden. Note: Description Acceptable The editor of a newspaper supporting this movement was convicted of libel after making an allegation of bribery against Auguste Burdeau. An essay about this battle begins by stating "this is a simple story of a battle; such a tale as may be told by a soldier who is no writer to a reader who is no soldier"; that Ambrose Bierce essay is titled "What I Saw of [this battle]." It ended with a Confederate raid on Fallen Timbers, where Nathan Bedford Forrest survived a shot to the pelvis. At this battle, Daniel Ruggles packed 50 cannons into a position referred to as the Hornet's Nest. Reinforcements led by Don Carlos Buell turned the tide at this battle, where P. G. T. Beauregard took over the Confederate army after Albert Sidney Johnston's death. Name this 1862 victory for Ulysses S. Grant's Union army, fought in southwestern Tennessee.

A rebellion among workers of this good resulted when they became angry at being fed oatmeal, canned peaches, and brown rice in the cafeteria, and those workers of it had to go to an "island of innocence" to access bars and brothels. The "American Village" housed workers of it in a failed utopian city called "Fordlandia." Quotas for producing this good were enforced by a Leon Rom-led group that brutally severed the hands of workers. This good was produced under the coercion of the Force Publique in the Belgian Congo. The process of vulcanization greatly increased demand for this good. Name this latex good that can be extracted from trees to make tires.

The Ostrogothic queen Amalasuntha was supposedly killed while performing this action. Constantine allegedly had his wife killed by suffocation while she was performing this activity. The hypocaust was created to help facilitate this activity. This activity usually involved proceeding to the caldarium from the tepidarium and frigidarium—an increase in temperature. The Romans generally performed this activity in public venues called thermae. Name this action which someone might use to cleanse their body.

A serial killer named for using these objects claimed to "crave the warmth of [his] native Tartarus" in a public announcement vowing to spare anyone who listened to jazz music; that person terrorized New Orleans' Italian-American community during his 1919 murder spree. This substance titles the third volume of The Venture of Islam, where Marshall Hodgson argued that this substance was vital to the creation of "military patronage states"—a hypothesis he articulated with William McNeill. The invention of this substance is legendarily attributed to a German called Berthold Schwarz. William of Rubruck may have brought this substance to Europe, since it appears in the Opus Majus of Roger Bacon. The three Islamic empires based on this substance were the Mughals, Safavids, and Ottomans. An early formula for this substance incorporated birthwort herb. This substance, whose original name means "fire medicine," helped end feudal society in Europe. Taoist alchemists likely used saltpeter and sulfur to create what explosive substance?

California senator William Knowland was nicknamed for his opposition to this country. John Service led the Dixie Mission to establish relations with the future leaders of this country. Leonard Hobhouse helped develop the economic theory that drove this party's policies. It created a "shopping list" of proposed policies in the Newcastle Programme. This party supported free school meals in its Provision of Meals Act. One of its "Terrible Twins" joked that "a fully equipped duke costs as much to keep as two dreadnoughts and they are just as great a terror." This party reduced the veto powers of the House of Lords since it blocked a key bill. This party held its last absolute majority after a landslide victory by Henry Campbell-Bannerman. This party tried to pass higher land taxes in the "People's Budget." This party expanded social welfare under H. H. Asquith, who led the U.K. At the start of World War I. Name this party which would later be eclipsed by the Labor party as the main enemies of the Conservatives.

One ruler of this dynasty met a woman selling nuts in the market and would later make that woman, Karin daughter of Mans, queen. That ruler of this dynasty supposedly had one shoulder lower than the other due to being dropped by a maid in infancy. One ruler of this dynasty had a tumultuous marriage with the daughter of the Elector of Brandenburg, Maria Eleonora. Hugo Grotius died in a shipwreck en-route to becoming a librarian for a ruler of this dynasty, whose cold castle may have caused the death of her tutor, Rene Descartes. This dynasty was ruled by the "Minerva of the North," who spent her early life under the regency of Axel Oxenstierna. Name this house whose Queen Christina was the daughter of Gustavus Adolphus.

Retaliatory massacres during this conflict occurred in the town of Tafas. The blockhouse of Abu al Lasan was the central point of a battle during this conflict won by Auda ibu Tayi. Sir Francis Drake brought many of this location's residents back to England. Virginia Dare was born at this site, where John White discovered the word "CROATOAN" carved into a tree trunk. The killing of prisoners in this city's jails by mobs was dubbed the "September Massacres." An insurrection in this city was quelled by a rising general in a "whiff of grapeshot." Some of the Fayuum mummy portraits depict examples of these objects "of justification" that symbolized success in the afterlife. Two of these objects colored red and white, which symbolized authority over Lower and Upper Egypt, combined to symbolize the Pharaoh's domain. Wiik nominated this man for the Nobel Peace Prize, and a radio station named in his honor was later taken over by The Jewish Daily Forward.
